claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that heat-inactivated VACV fails to rescue viral replication.

claims.claim: Heat-inactivated VACV can enter cells but cannot express its genes.
claims.source: Heat inactivated VACV, which can enter cells but cannot express its genes (Dales and Kajioka, 1964), failed to rescue VSV and SINV replication (Figure 3A), indicating that VACV gene expression was required for rescue.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claims.claim: Inhibiting post-replicative VACV gene expression with AraC did not prevent rescue of either VSV or SINV.
claims.source: We found that inhibiting post-replicative VACV gene expression did not prevent rescue of either VSV or SINV (Figure 3B), narrowing the RNA virus rescue activity to one or more of the 118 early VACV genes (Yang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-infection experiments with AraC treatment.

claims.claim: The RNA virus rescue activity is narrowed to one or more of the 118 early VACV genes.
claims.source: We found that inhibiting post-replicative VACV gene expression did not prevent rescue of either VSV or SINV (Figure 3B), narrowing the RNA virus rescue activity to one or more of the 118 early VACV genes (Yang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that AraC treatment does not prevent rescue, combined with knowledge about VACV gene expression timing.

claims.claim: VACV-MVA failed to fully rescue either VSV or SINV as compared to either VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains.
claims.source: We found that the attenuated modified VACV strain Ankara (VACV-MVA) (Antoine et al., 1998) failed to fully rescue either VSV or SINV as compared to either VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains (Figure 3C,D), despite similar levels of viral gene expression by all three VACV strains (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-infection experiments with different VACV strains.

claims.claim: VACV-WR, Copenhagen, and MVA strains showed similar levels of viral gene expression.
claims.source: We found that the attenuated modified VACV strain Ankara (VACV-MVA) (Antoine et al., 1998) failed to fully rescue either VSV or SINV as compared to either VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains (Figure 3C,D), despite similar levels of viral gene expression by all three VACV strains (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis.

claims.claim: VACV-MVA is defective for one or more factors required for RNA virus rescue in LD652 cells.
claims.source: These results suggested that VACV-MVA is defective for one or more factors required for RNA virus rescue in LD652 cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that VACV-MVA fails to fully rescue RNA viruses despite similar gene expression levels.

claims.claim: VACV-MVA has approximately 30 genes that are deleted or truncated relative to VACV-WR.
claims.source: The above findings narrowed the number of candidates to ∼30 genes that are deleted or truncated in VACV-MVA relative to VACV-WR (Meisinger-Henschel et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claims.claim: RNAi of A51R caused RNA virus gene expression to drop by approximately 95% for VSV and by approximately 69% for SINV.
claims.source: RNAi of a single, uncharacterized VACV gene, A51R, caused RNA virus gene expression to drop below an arbitrary cut off of 50% of the control (GFP) RNAi treatment. The A51R knockdown reduced virus gene expression by ∼95% (VSV) and by ∼69% (SINV) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments with LUC assays.

claims.claim: Co-infection with ΔA51R resulted in a 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression relative to co-infection with VACV-WR.
claims.source: Importantly, we found that co-infection with ΔA51R resulted in a 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression relative to co-infection with VACV-WR (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-infection experiments with deletion mutant virus.

claims.claim: VSV was rescued by co-infecting with revertant VACV strains expressing Flag-A51R.
claims.source: VSV was rescued by co-infecting with revertant VACV strains (Figure 4C), expressing a Flag-tagged A51R gene (Flag-A51R) reintroduced into either the A51R locus (ΔA51RFA51R) or the VACV thymidine kinase (J2R) locus (ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFA51R).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-infection experiments with revertant viruses.

claims.claim: Flag-A51R and Flag-MVAA51R proteins migrated as single bands of approximately 38 and 35 kDa, respectively, on immunoblots.
claims.source: Flag-A51R and Flag-MVAA51R proteins migrated as single bands of ∼38 and 35 kDa, respectively, on immunoblots (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis.

claims.claim: The lower molecular weight of the VACV-MVA A51R protein is likely due to a C-terminal truncation of approximately 20 amino acids that results from a genomic deletion that occurred during VACV-MVA passage in culture.
claims.source: The lower molecular weight of the VACV-MVA protein is likely due to a C-terminal truncation of ∼20 amino acids that results from a genomic deletion that occurred during VACV-MVA passage in culture (Antoine et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed molecular weight difference and knowledge from previous studies about VACV-MVA genomic deletions.

claims.claim: The VACV-MVA A51R protein is not functional.
claims.source: Furthermore, consistent with the idea that the VACV-MVA A51R protein is not functional, we found that the ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strain failed to fully rescue VSV (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that the strain expressing VACV-MVA A51R fails to rescue VSV.

claims.claim: Flag-A51R is expressed early in VACV infection.
claims.source: Importantly, immunoblot of lysates from a time course of A51RFA51R infection confirmed that Flag-A51R is expressed early in VACV infection, as it was detected by 2 hpi in the absence or presence of AraC (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis of time course experiments.

claims.claim: A51R is an early VACV protein necessary to relieve the restriction of VSV in LD652 cells.
claims.source: Together these results indicate that A51R is an early VACV protein necessary to relieve the restriction of VSV in LD652 cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing early expression of A51R and its requirement for VSV rescue.

claims.claim: A51R is required for full rescue of SINV replication by VACV.
claims.source: A51R was also required for full rescue of SINV replication by VACV (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-infection experiments.

claims.claim: ΔA51R and ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strains exhibited only a moderate fourfold reduction in their ability to promote SINV gene expression as compared to 100-fold reductions for VSV.
claims.source: However, we noticed that ΔA51R and ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strains exhibited only a moderate fourfold reduction in their ability to promote SINV gene expression as compared to 100-fold reductions for VSV (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-infection experiments comparing effects on VSV and SINV.

claims.claim: Other VACV factors in addition to A51R promote SINV replication in LD652 cells.
claims.source: These findings suggest that other VACV factors in addition to A51R promote SINV replication in LD652 cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that A51R deletion has a smaller effect on SINV than on VSV.

claims.claim: Expression of Flag-A51R resulted in an approximately 60-fold increase in VSV gene expression relative to control transfections.
claims.source: Although only ∼40–60% of cells expressed detectable Flag-A51R protein (data not shown), we observed an ∼60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections with empty p166 vector or vector encoding Flag-tagged GFP (Flag-GFP) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments with LUC assays.

claims.claim: Expression of Flag-A51R resulted in a 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections.
claims.source: Although only ∼40–60% of cells expressed detectable Flag-A51R protein (data not shown), we observed an ∼60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections with empty p166 vector or vector encoding Flag-tagged GFP (Flag-GFP) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments with LUC assays.

claims.claim: Approximately 40-60% of cells expressed detectable Flag-A51R protein after transfection.
claims.source: Although only ∼40–60% of cells expressed detectable Flag-A51R protein (data not shown), we observed an ∼60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections with empty p166 vector or vector encoding Flag-tagged GFP (Flag-GFP) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from microscopy (data not shown in manuscript).

claims.claim: VSV and SINV titers were enhanced by Flag-A51R transfection.
claims.source: VSV and SINV titers were similarly enhanced by Flag-A51R transfection (Figure 4G–H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from plaque assays.

claims.claim: Flag-A51R expression is sufficient to overcome the host restriction to RNA virus replication in the absence of other VACV proteins.
claims.source: These results indicate that Flag-A51R expression is sufficient to overcome the host restriction to RNA virus replication in the absence of other VACV proteins.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that transfection of A51R alone enhances viral replication.

claims.claim: Transfection of Flag-GFP or Flag-A51R constructs into LD652 cells did not lead to notable changes in cell viability over a 7 day time course.
claims.source: Transfection of Flag-GFP or Flag-A51R constructs into LD652 cells did not lead to notable changes in cell viability over a 7 day time course.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays.

claims.claim: When Flag-A51R-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC, cell viability began to drop by 96 hpi, ultimately reaching cell viabilities of approximately 50% by day 7 of infection.
claims.source: However, when transfected cells were subsequently infected with VSV-LUC, cell viability began to drop by 96 hpi, ultimately reaching cell viabilities of ∼50% by day 7 of infection (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays.

claims.claim: Reduced cell viability was not observed when Flag-GFP-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC.
claims.source: This reduced cell viability was not observed when Flag-GFP-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC, suggesting that active viral replication was required to induce cell death (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays.

claims.claim: Active viral replication is required to induce cell death in VSV-infected LD652 cells.
claims.source: This reduced cell viability was not observed when Flag-GFP-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC, suggesting that active viral replication was required to induce cell death (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that cell death only occurs when A51R is present to allow viral replication.

claims.claim: A51R genes are found in most vertebrate poxvirus genera.
claims.source: A51R genes are found in most vertebrate poxvirus genera (Table 1) yet absent in the genomes of entomopoxviruses (not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of poxvirus genomes.

claims.claim: A51R genes are absent in the genomes of entomopoxviruses.
claims.source: A51R genes are found in most vertebrate poxvirus genera (Table 1) yet absent in the genomes of entomopoxviruses (not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of poxvirus genomes.

claims.claim: A51R homologs from different poxviruses have amino acid identities ranging from 90% to 30% relative to VACV-WR A51R.
claims.source: We generated constructs to express some of these A51R homologs, with amino acid identities ranging from 90% to 30% relative to VACV-WR A51R (Table 1), and asked whether the ability of A51R to rescue VSV replication is conserved between poxvirus genera.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data.

claims.claim: A51R from each tested poxvirus enhanced VSV gene expression to a similar level.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that A51R from each poxvirus enhanced VSV gene expression to a similar level (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments with A51R homologs from different poxviruses.

claims.claim: The ability of A51R to overcome the LD652 restriction to VSV infection is a conserved function of distantly-related A51R homologs.
claims.source: Thus, the ability of A51R to overcome the LD652 restriction to VSV infection is a conserved function of distantly-related A51R homologs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that A51R homologs from different poxviruses all enhance VSV replication.

claims.claim: A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in L. dispar embryonic cell line (LdEP).
claims.source: Indeed, we found that A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in each of the three additional Lepidopteran cell lines tested, including an L. dispar embryonic cell line (LdEP) (Figure 6A), a Spodoptera frugiperda-derived cell line (Sf9) (Figure 6B,C), and a Manduca sexta-derived cell line (GV-1) (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-infection or transfection experiments in different cell lines.

claims.claim: A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in Spodoptera frugiperda-derived cell line (Sf9).
claims.source: Indeed, we found that A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in each of the three additional Lepidopteran cell lines tested, including an L. dispar embryonic cell line (LdEP) (Figure 6A), a Spodoptera frugiperda-derived cell line (Sf9) (Figure 6B,C), and a Manduca sexta-derived cell line (GV-1) (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments in different cell lines.

claims.claim: A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in Manduca sexta-derived cell line (GV-1).
claims.source: Indeed, we found that A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in each of the three additional Lepidopteran cell lines tested, including an L. dispar embryonic cell line (LdEP) (Figure 6A), a Spodoptera frugiperda-derived cell line (Sf9) (Figure 6B,C), and a Manduca sexta-derived cell line (GV-1) (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments in different cell lines.

claims.claim: A51R expression did not enhance VSV replication in D. melanogaster-derived DL1 cells.
claims.source: In contrast, A51R expression did not enhance VSV replication in D. melanogaster-derived DL1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), despite significant expression of Flag-A51R protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments in DL1 cells.

claims.claim: VSV gene expression in DL1 cells was not enhanced by co-infection with VACV-WR.
claims.source: VSV gene expression in DL1 cells was also not enhanced by co-infection with VACV-WR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-infection experiments in DL1 cells.

claims.claim: If Drosophila cells do have restrictions targeted by A51R, these restrictions are not sufficient to measurably check VSV replication.
claims.source: Thus, if Drosophila cells do have restrictions targeted by A51R, these restrictions are not sufficient to measurably check VSV replication in these experiments.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing no effect of A51R on VSV replication in Drosophila cells.

claims.claim: Flag-A51R formed both aggregate-like as well as filamentous structures in the cytoplasm of BSC-40 cells.
claims.source: We found that Flag-A51R, expressed under its natural promoter from the ΔA51RFA51R virus, formed both aggregate-like as well as filamentous structures in the cytoplasm of African green monkey-derived (BSC-40) cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy.

claims.claim: Flag-A51R staining pattern significantly overlapped with that of cellular tubulin.
claims.source: This staining pattern significantly overlapped with that of cellular tubulin, suggesting that A51R associates with a subset of MTs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy showing colocalization.

claims.claim: A51R associates with a subset of MTs.
claims.source: This staining pattern significantly overlapped with that of cellular tubulin, suggesting that A51R associates with a subset of MTs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing colocalization of A51R with tubulin.

claims.claim: Deconvolution of images revealed Flag-A51R staining localized on intact MT tracks.
claims.source: Indeed deconvolution of images from these experiments revealed Flag-A51R staining localized on intact MT tracks (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deconvolved confocal microscopy images.

claims.claim: In the presence of nocodazole, MT structures were essentially absent in mock-infected and ΔA51R-infected cells.
claims.source: In the presence of nocodazole, MT structures were essentially absent in mock-infected and ΔA51R-infected cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy of nocodazole-treated cells.

claims.claim: Filamentous, drug-resistant 'MT pieces' were abundant in ΔA51RFA51R-infected BSC-40 cells treated with nocodazole.
claims.source: However filamentous, drug-resistant 'MT pieces' were abundant in ΔA51RFA51R-infected BSC-40 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy of nocodazole-treated cells.

claims.claim: Nocodazole-resistant MT pieces were previously observed in mammalian cells infected with VACV-WR but not with VACV-MVA.
claims.source: Nocodazole-resistant MT pieces were previously observed in mammalian cells infected with VACV-WR but not with VACV-MVA (Ploubidou et al., 2000; Schepis et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claims.claim: Flag-MVAA51R stained small punctate structures throughout the cytoplasm that overlapped with tubulin in nocodazole-treated cells.
claims.source: We therefore examined Flag-MVAA51R protein localization in nocodazole-treated cells and found that, although Flag-MVAA51R staining stained small punctate structures throughout the cytoplasm that overlapped with tubulin, large drug-resistant MT-like structures failed to form (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy.

claims.claim: Large drug-resistant MT-like structures failed to form in cells expressing Flag-MVAA51R.
claims.source: We therefore examined Flag-MVAA51R protein localization in nocodazole-treated cells and found that, although Flag-MVAA51R staining stained small punctate structures throughout the cytoplasm that overlapped with tubulin, large drug-resistant MT-like structures failed to form (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy.

claims.claim: Flag-MVAA51R protein is deficient in its ability to both form filament-like structures and to protect MTs from depolymerization.
claims.source: These results suggest that Flag-MVAA51R protein is deficient in its ability to both form filament-like structures and to protect MTs from depolymerization.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing lack of drug-resistant MT structures with Flag-MVAA51R.

claims.claim: Flag-A51R expression is sufficient for both localization to, and stabilization of, MTs.
claims.source: To ask if Flag-A51R localization to and stabilization of MTs requires other VACV proteins, we transfected BSC-40 cells with a plasmid expressing Flag-A51R. We found that Flag-A51R expression was sufficient for both localization to, and stabilization of, MTs (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments with confocal microscopy.

claims.claim: A51R homologs from other poxviruses also co-localize with and protect MTs from depolymerization.
claims.source: Moreover, using similar assays, we found that A51R homologs from other poxviruses also co-localize with and protect MTs from depolymerization (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments with A51R homologs.

claims.claim: In LD652 cells, Flag-A51R formed aggregates and filamentous structures that co-localized with and protected MTs from depolymerization by vincristine.
claims.source: Finally, in LD652 cells, as in vertebrate cells, Flag-A51R formed aggregates and filamentous structures that co-localized with and protected MTs from depolymerization by the MT-depolymerizing agent vincristine (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments in LD652 cells with confocal microscopy.

claims.claim: The ability of A51R to interact with the host MT cytoskeleton is a conserved property of A51R proteins.
claims.source: Taken together, our findings suggest that the ability of A51R to interact with the host MT cytoskeleton is a conserved property of A51R proteins.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing MT interaction across different A51R homologs and cell types.

claims.claim: Alanine substitution of residue R321 produced a mutant with reduced VSV rescue phenotype compared to wild-type Flag-A51R.
claims.source: However, alanine substitution of residue R321, which lies within the C-terminal region of A51R that is missing in VACV-MVA A51R (Figure 8A), produced a suitable mutant for analysis. Flag-A51RR321A proteins displayed a reduced VSV rescue phenotype when compared to Flag-A51R proteins (Figure 8B) despite similar levels of expression (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis and transfection experiments.

claims.claim: Flag-A51R and Flag-A51RR321A both formed filamentous structures that overlapped with tubulin staining in the presence of vincristine.
claims.source: Importantly, when expressed in LD652 cells in the presence of vincristine, both Flag-A51R (Figure 8D; Video 1) and Flag-A51RR321A (Figure 8D; Video 2) formed filamentous structures that overlapped with tubulin staining (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfection experiments with confocal microscopy.

claims.claim: MT stabilization alone is insufficient to promote full RNA virus rescue.
claims.source: These results suggest that MT stabilization alone is insufficient to promote full RNA virus rescue.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that A51RR321A mutant stabilizes MTs but has reduced rescue activity.

claims.claim: The four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates are Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain, Ub, and ribosomal protein S15.
claims.source: Filtering differential normalized spectral abundance factor (NSAF) (Zybailov et al., 2006) values from both control and Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates identified the four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R treatments. These proteins are the target Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain (a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton [Clark et al., 2007]), Ub, and ribosomal protein S15 (a component of the 40S subunit of the ribosome that has also been shown to modulate the activity of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases [Daftuar et al., 2013]) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis.

claims.claim: Myosin II essential light chain is a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
claims.source: These proteins are the target Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain (a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton [Clark et al., 2007]), Ub, and ribosomal protein S15 (a component of the 40S subunit of the ribosome that has also been shown to modulate the activity of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases [Daftuar et al., 2013]) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claims.claim: Ribosomal protein S15 is a component of the 40S subunit of the ribosome.
claims.source: These proteins are the target Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain (a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton [Clark et al., 2007]), Ub, and ribosomal protein S15 (a component of the 40S subunit of the ribosome that has also been shown to modulate the activity of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases [Daftuar et al., 2013]) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claims.claim: Ribosomal protein S15 has been shown to modulate the activity of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases.
claims.source: These proteins are the target Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain (a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton [Clark et al., 2007]), Ub, and ribosomal protein S15 (a component of the 40S subunit of the ribosome that has also been shown to modulate the activity of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases [Daftuar et al., 2013]) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claims.claim: The majority of A51R associated with insoluble cell fractions.
claims.source: Unfortunately we found that the majority of A51R associated with insoluble cell fractions, making direct immunoblot analysis of immunoprecipitated materials impossible.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations during immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: Radiolabeled VSV N protein was undetectable in cells infected only with either VACV-WR or VSV-LUC.
claims.source: We found that radiolabeled VSV N protein was undetectable in cells infected only with either VACV-WR (control) or VSV-LUC.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from radiolabeling and immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: Significant quantities of radiolabeled VSV N protein were found in VSV-LUC-infected cells that were also infected with either VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains.
claims.source: In contrast, we found significant quantities of radiolabeled VSV N protein in VSV-LUC-infected cells that were also infected with either VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains (Figure 9A, top panel).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from radiolabeling and immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: Viral protein translation rates are too low to be detected by radiolabeling in VSV-LUC single infections but are detectable in co-infections with VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains.
claims.source: These results suggest that viral protein translation rates are too low to be detected by this method in VSV-LUC single infections but are detectable (and surprisingly similar) in co-infections with VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing similar levels of newly synthesized protein in both co-infection conditions.

claims.claim: VSV N was not detected in either VACV-WR or VSV-LUC single infection lysates by immunoblot.
claims.source: When whole cell extracts from these experiments were immunoblotted for total VSV N protein levels, again we found that VSV N was not detected in either VACV-WR or VSV-LUC single infection lysates.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis.

claims.claim: Total VSV N protein levels were dramatically reduced in ΔA51R co-infections compared to co-infections with VACV-WR.
claims.source: However, total VSV N protein levels were dramatically reduced in ΔA51R co-infections compared to co-infections with VACV-WR (Figure 9A, middle panel).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot analysis.

claims.claim: The levels of radiolabeled VSV N protein appeared to diminish more rapidly during ΔA51R co-infection than during VACV-WR co-infection.
claims.source: Although newly synthesized VSV N protein could be detected during co-infection with either VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains (Figure 9B), the levels of radiolabeled protein appeared to diminish more rapidly during ΔA51R co-infection (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pulse-chase experiments.

claims.claim: The half-life of VSV N is approximately 5.3 hours during co-infection with VACV-WR.
claims.source: Regression analyses of pulse-chase experiments estimated the half-life of VSV N to be ∼5.3 hr during co-infection with VACV-WR while only ∼1.8 hr during co-infection with the ΔA51R strain.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pulse-chase experiments and regression analysis.

claims.claim: The half-life of VSV N is approximately 1.8 hours during co-infection with the ΔA51R strain.
claims.source: Regression analyses of pulse-chase experiments estimated the half-life of VSV N to be ∼5.3 hr during co-infection with VACV-WR while only ∼1.8 hr during co-infection with the ΔA51R strain.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pulse-chase experiments and regression analysis.

claims.claim: A51R associates with Ub and promotes viral protein stability.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that A51R associates with Ub and promotes viral protein stability.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing A51R-Ub association and increased viral protein half-life in presence of A51R.

claims.claim: At a low MOI of 0.03, the ΔA51R, VACV-WR, and ΔA51RFA51R strains replicated with similar kinetics until 24 hpi.
claims.source: At a low MOI of 0.03, the ΔA51R, VACV-WR, and ΔA51RFA51R strains replicated with similar kinetics until 24 hpi at which point ΔA51R titers began to plateau.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from growth curve analyses.

claims.claim: ΔA51R titers began to plateau at 24 hpi while VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers continued to increase to approximately 100-fold higher levels by 72 hpi.
claims.source: At a low MOI of 0.03, the ΔA51R, VACV-WR, and ΔA51RFA51R strains replicated with similar kinetics until 24 hpi at which point ΔA51R titers began to plateau. In contrast, VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers continued to increase to ∼100-fold higher levels by 72 hpi (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from growth curve analyses.

claims.claim: The plateau of ΔA51R titer was also observed at a higher MOI of 3, but occurred earlier, at 12 hpi.
claims.source: This plateau of ΔA51R titer was also observed at a higher MOI of 3, but occurred earlier, at 12 hpi (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from growth curve analyses at different MOIs.

claims.claim: A51R promotes VACV replication in vertebrate cell culture.
claims.source: These results indicate that A51R promotes VACV replication in vertebrate cell culture.

results.result: VSV and SINV are restricted in their replication after entry into Lepidopteran LD652 cells, with less than 4% of cells showing GFP fluorescence by 96 hpi at MOI 10. Viral capsids and transcripts are detected inside cells at early time points, and rescue can occur even when VACV is added 24 hours post-infection, indicating post-entry restriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15, C19, C20, C21, and C22 are well-supported by multiple experimental approaches including fluorescence microscopy (C15), confocal microscopy showing viral capsids inside cells (C19), RT-PCR detecting viral transcripts (C20), and time-course rescue experiments (C21). The convergence of these independent lines of evidence strongly supports the conclusion of post-entry restriction (C22).

results.result: VACV co-infection overcomes the restriction of VSV and SINV replication in LD652 cells, increasing GFP-positive cells to approximately 77% for VSV and 45% for SINV by 96 hpi. This rescue requires VACV gene expression, specifically early gene expression, as heat-inactivated VACV fails to rescue and AraC treatment (blocking late genes) does not prevent rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C16, C48, C49, C51, and C52 are supported by complementary experimental data: fluorescence microscopy quantification (C16), heat-inactivation experiments (C48-C49), and AraC treatment experiments (C51-C52). The logical progression from demonstrating rescue to narrowing down the requirement to early VACV genes is sound and well-controlled.

results.result: Lepidopteran RNAi pathways restrict RNA virus infection, as demonstrated by RNAi knockdown of AGO2 and Dicer-2 increasing viral gene expression approximately 10-fold. This is consistent with the conservation of RNAi-based antiviral immunity across vertebrates and invertebrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C30, C31, and C164 are supported by RNAi knockdown experiments showing increased viral replication upon silencing of key RNAi pathway components. The ~10-fold increase in LUC expression is a substantial effect. The consistency with known RNAi antiviral functions (C164) provides additional support, though the magnitude of effect is modest compared to ubiquitin pathway components.

results.result: Lepidopteran NF-κB pathways restrict RNA virus infection, as RNAi knockdown of Relish (NF-κB homolog) increased viral gene expression approximately 10-fold. This suggests an IMD-like pathway protects against virus infection in Lepidoptera, consistent with the known role of Relish in the Drosophila IMD pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C32, and C171 are supported by RNAi knockdown data showing ~10-fold increase in viral replication. Claims C168-C170 provide established background knowledge about the IMD pathway. The inference that an IMD-like pathway operates in Lepidoptera (C171) is reasonable given the functional conservation of Relish, though direct mechanistic evidence for pathway activation is not provided.

results.result: Lepidopteran ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection. RNAi knockdown of Effete and ubiquitin-encoding genes (Polyubiquitin, Ub-RPL40, Ub-RPS27A) increased viral gene expression up to 1000-fold for VSV and 10-fold for SINV. Multiple UPS inhibition approaches (Ub RNAi, PYR-41, MG132, PLpro expression) enhanced viral-driven but not plasmid-driven LUC expression, indicating specificity for viral replication rather than general LUC protein stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C33-C35, C39-C44, and C47 are strongly supported by convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches: RNAi knockdown, chemical inhibitors (PYR-41, MG132), and expression of a viral deubiquitinase (PLpro). The dramatic 1000-fold effect for VSV with ubiquitin RNAi is particularly striking. The control experiments showing no effect on plasmid-driven LUC expression (C39-C44) effectively rule out artifacts related to LUC protein stability.

results.result: VACV protein A51R is necessary for RNA virus rescue in LD652 cells. RNAi of A51R reduced viral gene expression by ~95% for VSV and ~69% for SINV. Genetic deletion of A51R (ΔA51R strain) resulted in 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression, which was rescued by revertant strains expressing Flag-A51R. The truncated VACV-MVA A51R protein is non-functional. A51R is expressed early in VACV infection and is required for full rescue of both VSV and SINV, though other VACV factors also contribute to SINV rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C57-C59, C62, C64-C67 are well-supported by complementary genetic approaches: RNAi knockdown (C57), gene deletion (C58), genetic reversion (C59), and comparison with VACV-MVA (C62). The convergence of multiple independent genetic manipulations all pointing to A51R as necessary for rescue provides strong evidence. The observation that A51R deletion has a smaller effect on SINV than VSV (C66-C67) is appropriately interpreted as suggesting additional VACV factors contribute to SINV rescue.

results.result: Expression of Flag-A51R alone is sufficient to overcome host restriction to RNA virus replication in LD652 cells, resulting in approximately 60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression, as well as enhanced virus titers. Transfection of Flag-A51R or Flag-GFP alone does not affect cell viability, but Flag-A51R-transfected cells infected with VSV show reduced viability by 96 hpi, reaching ~50% viability by day 7, indicating that active viral replication is required for cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69, C71-C76 are supported by transfection experiments showing that A51R expression alone (without other VACV proteins) is sufficient to enhance viral replication. The ~60-fold increase for VSV is substantial, though lower than the effect seen with full VACV co-infection. The cell viability experiments (C73-C76) provide important controls showing that A51R itself is not toxic and that cell death requires active viral replication, supporting the interpretation that A51R enables productive infection.

results.result: A51R genes are found in most vertebrate poxvirus genera but absent in entomopoxviruses. A51R homologs from different poxviruses (with amino acid identities ranging from 90% to 30% relative to VACV-WR A51R) all enhanced VSV gene expression to similar levels, indicating that the ability to overcome LD652 restriction to VSV infection is a conserved function of distantly-related A51R homologs.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by bioinformatic analysis (C77-C79) and functional experiments with A51R homologs from multiple poxviruses (C80). The conservation of function across homologs with as little as 30% amino acid identity is striking and suggests strong selective pressure to maintain this activity. The experimental design testing multiple homologs is appropriate for assessing functional conservation.

results.result: A51R expression relieves restriction to VSV replication in multiple Lepidopteran cell lines (L. dispar LdEP, Spodoptera frugiperda Sf9, and Manduca sexta GV-1) but not in Drosophila melanogaster DL1 cells. VACV-WR co-infection also does not enhance VSV replication in DL1 cells, suggesting that if Drosophila cells have restrictions targeted by A51R, they are not sufficient to measurably check VSV replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 are supported by experiments in multiple cell lines showing A51R function is conserved across Lepidopteran species but not in Diptera. This phylogenetic pattern is informative about the evolution and specificity of A51R function. The negative result in Drosophila cells (C85-C87) is appropriately interpreted with caution, acknowledging that absence of effect could have multiple explanations.

results.result: A51R colocalizes with host microtubules, forming both aggregate-like and filamentous structures in the cytoplasm. Flag-A51R staining significantly overlaps with cellular tubulin, and deconvolution reveals A51R localized on intact MT tracks. In the presence of nocodazole, filamentous drug-resistant 'MT pieces' are abundant in ΔA51RFA51R-infected cells but absent in mock-infected and ΔA51R-infected cells. The truncated VACV-MVA A51R protein fails to form large drug-resistant MT-like structures, suggesting it is deficient in both forming filament-like structures and protecting MTs from depolymerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C88-C97 are well-supported by confocal microscopy showing colocalization with tubulin (C89), deconvolved images showing localization on MT tracks (C91), and drug resistance experiments with nocodazole (C92-C93). The comparison with VACV-MVA A51R (C95-C97) provides important negative control data. The convergence of multiple imaging approaches and the consistency with previous observations in the literature (C94) strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: A51R stabilizes host microtubules, as demonstrated by the presence of nocodazole-resistant and vincristine-resistant microtubule structures in A51R-expressing cells. Flag-A51R expression alone is sufficient for both localization to and stabilization of MTs, without requiring other VACV proteins. This ability to interact with the host MT cytoskeleton is conserved across A51R homologs from other poxviruses and functions in both vertebrate and Lepidopteran cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C93, C98-C101 are supported by drug resistance experiments with nocodazole and vincristine showing MT stabilization. The sufficiency experiments (C98) demonstrate that A51R alone can stabilize MTs without other viral proteins. The conservation across homologs (C99) and cell types (C100) indicates this is a fundamental property of A51R proteins. The convergence of evidence from multiple drugs, cell types, and A51R homologs provides strong support.

results.result: A51R associates with ubiquitin, as demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis showing ubiquitin as one of the four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates. The majority of A51R associates with insoluble cell fractions, making direct immunoblot analysis difficult. Collectively, data suggest that A51R associates with Ub and promotes viral protein stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C105, C109, and C118 are supported by mass spectrometry data identifying ubiquitin in A51R immunoprecipitates (C105). The technical challenge of A51R insolubility (C109) is acknowledged, which explains why direct immunoblot confirmation was not possible. The inference that A51R associates with Ub and promotes viral protein stability (C118) is reasonable given the mass spec data combined with the protein stability data, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: A51R promotes viral protein stability without affecting viral mRNA translation rates. Radiolabeling experiments show similar levels of newly synthesized VSV N protein during co-infection with VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains, but total VSV N protein levels are dramatically reduced in ΔA51R co-infections. Pulse-chase experiments reveal that the half-life of VSV N is approximately 5.3 hours during VACV-WR co-infection but only approximately 1.8 hours during ΔA51R co-infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C110-C117 are supported by complementary radiolabeling approaches: pulse-labeling to measure translation rates (C110-C112) and pulse-chase to measure protein stability (C115-C117). The finding that translation rates are similar but protein stability differs between VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections provides strong evidence that A51R acts post-translationally to stabilize viral proteins. The quantitative half-life measurements (C116-C117) provide precise estimates of the magnitude of the effect.

results.result: A51R does not affect viral mRNA translation rates, as demonstrated by radiolabeling experiments showing similar levels of newly synthesized VSV N protein during co-infection with VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains, though translation rates in single infections are too low to detect by this method.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C110-C112 are supported by pulse-labeling experiments showing similar amounts of newly synthesized radiolabeled VSV N protein in both VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections. This is an important control that helps localize A51R function to post-translational protein stability rather than effects on translation. The inability to detect translation in single infections (C110, C112) is a limitation but does not undermine the comparison between the two co-infection conditions.

results.result: An A51R point mutant (R321A) shows reduced VSV rescue activity compared to wild-type Flag-A51R, despite similar expression levels. Both Flag-A51R and Flag-A51RR321A form filamentous structures that overlap with tubulin staining in the presence of vincristine, suggesting that MT stabilization alone is insufficient to promote full RNA virus rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by mutagenesis experiments showing separation of function: the R321A mutant retains MT-stabilizing activity (C103) but has reduced rescue activity (C102). This is strong evidence that A51R has functions beyond MT stabilization that are required for full viral rescue (C104). The similar expression levels of wild-type and mutant proteins (C102) rule out the trivial explanation that reduced activity is due to reduced expression.

results.result: A51R is critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells. At low MOI (0.03), ΔA51R, VACV-WR, and ΔA51RFA51R strains replicate with similar kinetics until 24 hpi, at which point ΔA51R titers plateau while VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers continue to increase to approximately 100-fold higher levels by 72 hpi. This plateau occurs earlier (12 hpi) at higher MOI (3).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C119-C122 are supported by growth curve analyses at multiple MOIs showing that ΔA51R replication plateaus while wild-type and revertant strains continue to replicate. The ~100-fold difference in titers by 72 hpi is substantial. The MOI-dependent timing of the plateau (C121) provides additional insight into the kinetics of the defect. The revertant strain control (C119-C120) confirms that the phenotype is specifically due to A51R deletion.

results.result: A51R is critical for VACV pathogenesis in mice. VACV-WR infection causes rapid weight loss and 100% mortality by day 7, while only 1/5 ΔA51R-infected animals die by day 7, with the remainder recovering and surviving 28 days. The ΔA51R virus displays attenuated virulence at multiple doses. Both viruses replicate to similar titers in lungs by day 4, but by day 6, significantly higher titers (p<0.05) are detected in ovaries of VACV-WR-infected animals compared to ΔA51R-infected animals (virus detectable in only 1/5).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C123-C132 are strongly supported by in vivo mouse infection studies showing dramatic differences in mortality (C124-C125), confirmation at multiple doses (C126), and tissue-specific viral loads (C127-C131). The statistical significance of differences in ovarian viral loads (C130) and the pattern of similar replication in lungs but reduced spread to distant tissues (C129-C131) provide mechanistic insight. The convergence of survival, weight loss, and tissue titer data provides robust evidence for A51R as a virulence factor.

results.result: The reduced replication of the ΔA51R strain at later time points is not caused by a reduction in extracellular enveloped virus (EEV), which primarily mediates viral spread. Despite approximately 10-fold lower total virus titers, ΔA51R cultures shed approximately twofold higher levels of EEV than VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R cultures.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C135 are supported by EEV titration experiments showing paradoxically higher EEV release from ΔA51R-infected cells despite lower total virus titers. This is an important control ruling out defects in EEV production as the explanation for reduced spread. The observation that ΔA51R releases more EEV (C135) is counterintuitive and suggests A51R may actually limit EEV release, which is discussed in the context of immune evasion.

results.result: IFN pre-treatment reduces VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers by approximately 10-fold by 24 hpi, and ΔA51R titers are similarly reduced, suggesting that loss of A51R does not make VACV more susceptible to the antiviral effects of IFN.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C138 are supported by IFN pre-treatment experiments showing similar fold-reduction in titers for all three virus strains. This is an important control ruling out increased IFN sensitivity as the mechanism for ΔA51R attenuation. The similar response to IFN (C137-C138) suggests A51R functions through IFN-independent mechanisms, consistent with the lack of effect of E3L/B18R deletion in Lepidopteran cells.

results.result: A51R may inhibit Ub-dependent host targeting of viral proteins for degradation. The association of A51R with Ub, combined with A51R-dependent viral protein stabilization and the role of the UPS in restricting viral replication, points to a role for A51R in usurping or inhibiting host Ub machinery. A51R-dependent sequestration of Ub or removal of Ub from viral proteins might overcome a Ub-dependent mechanism that activates host antiviral effectors or targets viral proteins for destruction.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C178-C179, C191, and C216 are speculative mechanistic proposals based on circumstantial evidence: A51R associates with Ub (C11), promotes viral protein stability (C12), and the UPS restricts viral replication (C5). While these observations are consistent with the proposed mechanism, direct evidence for Ub sequestration, deubiquitination activity, or inhibition of specific E3 ligases is not provided. The mechanism remains uncertain and requires additional biochemical characterization.

results.result: Actinomycin D at 0.1 μg/ml reduces LD652 cell viability by approximately 50% after 48 hours, and higher doses enhance viral gene expression by up to approximately 100-fold, suggesting that host cell transcription is required for LD652 resistance to RNA virus infection and that LD652 cells express antiviral immunity factors. The enhanced replication may be partly due to apoptosis induction, as ActD can induce apoptosis in invertebrate cells and apoptosis enhances SINV replication in mosquitoes.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 are supported by cell viability assays and LUC assays showing dose-dependent effects of ActD. The inference that host transcription is required for antiviral responses (C25-C26) is reasonable given that ActD blocks transcription and enhances viral replication. However, the alternative explanation involving apoptosis (C27-C29) is appropriately acknowledged as a confounding factor. The inability to definitively separate transcriptional inhibition from apoptosis induction is a limitation, making the mechanistic interpretation somewhat uncertain.

results.result: VACV-MVA fails to fully rescue VSV or SINV compared to VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains, despite similar levels of viral gene expression by all three strains. This suggests VACV-MVA is defective for one or more factors required for RNA virus rescue, narrowing candidates to approximately 30 genes that are deleted or truncated in VACV-MVA relative to VACV-WR.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by co-infection experiments with different VACV strains showing differential rescue activity (C53) despite similar gene expression levels (C54). This is an important observation that helped narrow the search for rescue factors. The inference that VACV-MVA is defective for rescue factors (C55) is sound, and the narrowing to ~30 candidate genes (C56) based on known genomic differences is a logical approach that ultimately led to identification of A51R.

results.result: Flag-A51R and Flag-MVAA51R proteins migrate as single bands of approximately 38 and 35 kDa respectively on immunoblots. The lower molecular weight of the VACV-MVA A51R protein is likely due to a C-terminal truncation of approximately 20 amino acids from a genomic deletion during VACV-MVA passage. The VACV-MVA A51R protein is not functional, as the ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strain fails to fully rescue VSV.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by immunoblot data showing different molecular weights (C60), knowledge of VACV-MVA genomic deletions (C61), and functional rescue experiments (C62). The inference that the C-terminal truncation explains the molecular weight difference (C61) is reasonable. The conclusion that VACV-MVA A51R is non-functional (C62) is well-supported by the failure of the ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strain to rescue VSV, providing important negative control data.

results.result: Flag-A51R is expressed early in VACV infection, detected by 2 hpi in the absence or presence of AraC. Together with genetic data, this indicates A51R is an early VACV protein necessary to relieve the restriction of VSV in LD652 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are supported by time-course immunoblot experiments showing early expression (C63). The detection of A51R at 2 hpi both with and without AraC confirms it is an early gene product. This timing is consistent with the AraC experiments showing that early gene expression is sufficient for rescue (C51-C52) and helps establish A51R as the relevant early gene.

results.result: A51R co-sediments with MTs in MT-pelleting assays (unpublished data), suggesting close interaction with MT structures. The presence or absence of functional A51R could explain why nocodazole-resistant 'MT pieces' were observed in VACV-infected cells but not in uninfected or VACV-MVA-infected cells. These results suggest A51R is the elusive MT-stabilizing factor encoded by VACV.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C194 are supported by unpublished MT-pelleting data (C192) and the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: A51R colocalizes with MTs (C9), stabilizes MTs (C10), and VACV-MVA A51R (which is truncated) fails to stabilize MTs (C96-C97). The connection to previous observations of nocodazole-resistant MT pieces in VACV-infected cells (C193-C194) provides strong circumstantial support that A51R is the responsible factor, though the unpublished pelleting data limits full evaluation.

results.result: Previous studies implicate MTs in promoting VSV and SINV gene expression, and tubulin promotes VSV RNA polymerase activity in vitro. VSV transport to the cell surface is MT-dependent. However, a recent study found no effect of MT depolymerization on VSV and SINV replication, leaving the role of MTs unresolved. Given the very early restriction of RNA virus gene expression in LD652 cells, it seems unlikely that A51R overcomes host restriction by promoting RNA virus transport on stabilized MTs.
results.evaluation: Claims C195-C200 appropriately summarize conflicting literature on the role of MTs in VSV/SINV replication (C195-C199) and draw a reasonable inference (C200) that MT-dependent transport is unlikely to explain A51R function given the early timing of restriction. This reasoning is sound - if restriction occurs very early post-entry, then effects on later transport steps would not explain rescue. The acknowledgment of conflicting literature (C199) is appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The A51RR321A mutant studies do not rule out that MT-association is required for A51R immunosuppressive function or stability. A51R may subvert host antiviral responses by perturbing MT-dependent transport of host factors/organelles. VACV-WR infection causes endosome redistribution to perinuclear clusters, requiring early gene expression and activities lacking in VACV-MVA. A51R fits these criteria and could induce endosome clustering to overcome host mechanisms that trap viruses in endosomes. Punctate VSV N and SINV E1 staining at 24 hpi may represent virions trapped in endosomes, as both viruses can use endocytic entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C201-C208 are largely speculative (C202, C205, C207) or acknowledge limitations (C201). While the observations about endosome clustering (C203-C204) and punctate viral protein staining (C206) are factual, the connections to A51R function are inferential. The hypothesis that A51R perturbs endosomal trafficking (C202, C205) is plausible given A51R's MT-stabilizing activity and the known role of MTs in endosomal transport, but direct evidence is lacking. These remain interesting hypotheses requiring further testing.

results.result: Alteration of MT-dependent trafficking by A51R may explain why VACV-MVA and ΔA51R strains release 2-3 times more EEV than VACV-WR. EEV release is MT-dependent and elicits neutralizing antibodies. A51R may attenuate virion transport along MTs and EEV release to allow immune escape. The Dryvax vaccine strain encodes a fragmented A51R gene, raising the possibility that loss of A51R function contributes to poxvirus immunity induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C209-C214 are largely speculative connections between A51R function, EEV release, and vaccine efficacy. While the observations about increased EEV release from ΔA51R (C135) and Dryvax having fragmented A51R (C213) are factual, the mechanistic explanations (C209, C212) and implications for vaccination (C214) are speculative. The hypothesis is internally consistent and plausible, but lacks direct experimental support. This represents interesting speculation for future work rather than established findings.

results.result: MT structures might serve as a scaffold allowing A51R to interact with and sequester host factors like Ub. A51R-dependent sequestration of Ub or removal of Ub from viral proteins might overcome Ub-dependent mechanisms that activate host antiviral effectors or target viral proteins for destruction. This predicts Lepidopteran cells might have a mechanism to target protein synthesis coupled to cytoplasmic transcription, which is not unreasonable given that VACV, VSV, and SINV all replicate cytoplasmically while plasmid-based transcription occurs in the nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C215-C218 are speculative mechanistic proposals. While the observations that support these hypotheses are sound (A51R associates with MTs and Ub, promotes viral protein stability, and UPS inhibition specifically enhances viral but not plasmid-driven LUC expression), the specific mechanisms proposed (Ub sequestration on MT scaffolds, targeting of cytoplasmic translation) lack direct experimental support. These are reasonable hypotheses that explain the data but require biochemical validation.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about virus biology, cell biology, and prior literature. These include established facts about VACV infection in LD652 cells, poxvirus immunomodulatory proteins, ribosomal protein structure, proteasome inhibitors, invertebrate model systems, RNAi pathways, Lepidopteran virus studies, the IMD pathway, ubiquitin functions, viral deubiquitinases, IFN responses, and cytoplasmic replication of VACV/VSV/SINV.
results.evaluation: These claims (C17-C18, C36-C38, C45-C46, C50, C106-C108, C134, C139-C177, C181-C182, C218) represent established scientific knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. They provide necessary context and background for interpreting the experimental findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with established understanding in virology, cell biology, and immunology.

results.result: Speculative claims about future applications and significance. A new model system for studying RNA viruses in Lepidopteran hosts may be useful for designing biocontrol agents and improving understanding of RNA virus disease in vertebrates. The restrictive nature of VSV/SINV infections in L. dispar cells may prove useful for identifying additional immunomodulators. Further A51R studies will help understand eukaryotic antiviral immunity and may provide strategies to overcome antiviral responses in Lepidopteran pests. The uncoupling of RNA virus restriction by A51R provides a new arena to explore virus-host interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C162, C185, C219-C221 are speculative statements about potential future applications and significance of the work. While these are reasonable projections based on the findings, they represent possibilities rather than demonstrated outcomes. These forward-looking statements are appropriate for a discussion section but do not constitute results that can be evaluated as supported or unsupported.

results.result: Interpretive claims about the significance and implications of findings. Transient expression of nodamura virus B2 protein rescues VSV and SINV replication in Lepidopteran cell lines (unpublished). Lepidopteran cells provide a new system to investigate antiviral RNAi. This is the first example of heterologous virus rescue by a vertebrate virus in an invertebrate host. E3L/B18R deletion had no effect on VACV-dependent VSV rescue in L. dispar cells. Additional VACV proteins likely contribute to suppression of antiviral activity. A51R-mediated rescue occurs post-entry. A51R overcomes immunity mechanisms shared between Lepidopterans and mammals but absent/easily antagonized in Diptera. The conservation of RNA virus rescue and MT association across A51R homologs suggests both functions may be important for poxvirus replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C165, C167, C180, C183-C184, C186-C190 represent interpretive conclusions drawn from the experimental data. Most are well-supported by the data: C165 by unpublished experiments, C180 by literature knowledge, C183 by unpublished data, C184 by partial rescue with ΔA51R, C186 by entry/transcription data, C187 by cell-type specificity, C188 by conservation across homologs. Claims C189-C190 about both functions being important for poxvirus replication are more speculative but supported by the in vivo attenuation data.

results.result: VSV and SINV are restricted in their replication after entry into Lepidopteran LD652 cells, showing <4% GFP-positive cells at 96 hpi. This restriction is overcome by VACV co-infection, increasing GFP-positive cells to ~77% (VSV) and ~45% (SINV). Viral capsids and transcripts are detected inside cells, and rescue can occur even when VACV is added 24 hours post-infection, indicating post-entry restriction.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises a critical concern about the interpretation of post-entry restriction, specifically noting that 'the observation of E1 staining in a punctate pattern inside the cell at 24 hpi indicates that the virus has been taken up by endocytosis but is trapped in endosomes.' The reviewer states this is 'the only way to explain why the E1 protein, a transmembrane protein, is present inside the cells,' suggesting the authors may have missed an important clue about endosomal trapping rather than a later post-entry block. This challenges the authors' conclusion about where the restriction occurs.

results.result: RNAi screening identified that Lepidopteran RNAi pathways (AGO2, Dicer-2), NF-κB pathways (Relish), and ubiquitin-proteasome pathways (Effete, ubiquitin-encoding genes) restrict RNA virus infection in LD652 cells. Knockdown of these factors increased viral gene expression by ~10-fold to nearly 1000-fold.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about host restriction pathways. The manuscript is described as making 'novel insights into the nature of RNA virus restriction in lepidopteran cells' and reviewers note that 'the findings are an important contribution to our knowledge of anti-viral responses in these organisms.' The RNAi screening results identifying multiple restriction pathways are accepted without specific critique.

results.result: VACV protein A51R is necessary and sufficient for rescuing RNA virus replication in Lepidopteran cells. RNAi knockdown of A51R reduced viral gene expression by ~95% (VSV) and ~69% (SINV). Deletion of A51R (ΔA51R) resulted in 100-fold reduction in VSV rescue, which was restored by revertant strains. Transfection of A51R alone increased VSV gene expression ~60-fold and SINV ~12-fold.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as a key finding, stating 'The authors identify a previously uncharacterized VACV gene product A51R as being responsible for the rescue of RNA viral infection.' This is treated as one of the manuscript's major discoveries without challenge to the experimental evidence demonstrating A51R's necessity and sufficiency.

results.result: A51R colocalizes with and stabilizes host microtubules. Flag-A51R formed filamentous structures overlapping with tubulin staining and protected microtubules from depolymerization by nocodazole and vincristine. This property is conserved across A51R homologs from different poxviruses and occurs in both vertebrate and Lepidopteran cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge, noting that 'A51R colocalizes with, and stabilizes, host microtubules' as part of the manuscript's contributions. The microtubule stabilization data is discussed as one of the 'important clues' about A51R function. No concerns are raised about the microscopy or drug resistance experiments demonstrating MT stabilization.

results.result: A51R associates with ubiquitin. Mass spectrometry analysis identified ubiquitin as one of the most enriched proteins in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates. This association, combined with protein stability data, suggests A51R promotes viral protein stability.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding, stating 'A51R...also associates with ubiquitin' as part of the manuscript's discoveries. The ubiquitin association is treated as an established result that contributes to understanding A51R's mechanism, though reviewers note the mechanism remains 'complex' and will require 'future detailed characterizations.'

results.result: A51R promotes viral protein stability without affecting translation rates. Pulse-labeling showed similar levels of newly synthesized VSV N protein in VACV-WR and ΔA51R co-infections, but total VSV N protein levels were dramatically reduced in ΔA51R co-infections. Pulse-chase experiments estimated VSV N half-life at ~5.3 hr with VACV-WR versus ~1.8 hr with ΔA51R.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 directly challenges this conclusion, stating 'The authors conclude that A51R may act in part by promoting the stability of viral proteins, but the evidence here is not convincing.' The reviewer notes that reduced protein levels 'could be due to the 100-fold decreased replication of VSV in cells infected with A51R mutant vs wt vaccinia' and requests 'a proper pulse-chase experiment to properly determine the half life of N in cells infected with wt vs A51R mutant vaccinia (and preferably also in cells transfected with A51R in the absence of other viral genes).'

results.result: A51R is critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells. Growth curve analyses showed that ΔA51R titers plateaued at 24 hpi (MOI 0.03) or 12 hpi (MOI 3), while VACV-WR and revertant strains continued to increase to ~100-fold higher levels by 72 hpi.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge, noting that the manuscript shows 'A51R is also critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells' as one of its contributions. The growth curve data demonstrating reduced replication of ΔA51R is treated as established evidence supporting A51R's importance in vertebrate infections.

results.result: A51R is critical for VACV pathogenesis in mice. VACV-WR infection caused 100% mortality by day 7, while only 1/5 ΔA51R-infected animals died and the rest recovered. By day 6, significantly higher virus titers were detected in ovaries of VACV-WR-infected animals compared to ΔA51R-infected animals (p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding, noting 'A51R is also critical...for pathogenesis in mice' and that 'VACV lacking functional A51R is attenuated and this may be an important feature of the vaccine strain of the virus, which has a truncation of A51R.' The in vivo pathogenesis data is treated as convincing evidence without specific critique of the experimental design or interpretation.

results.result: The A51RR321A mutant has reduced VSV rescue activity compared to wild-type A51R despite retaining the ability to form filamentous structures and stabilize microtubules in the presence of vincristine, suggesting that MT stabilization alone is insufficient for full RNA virus rescue.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this mutant analysis. The finding that MT stabilization is insufficient for full rescue is consistent with reviewers' acknowledgment that 'the mechanism(s) by which A51R relieves the restriction of VSV and SINV is still vague, but there are important clues that can be followed in future work.' The mutant data is accepted as providing insight into separable functions of A51R.

results.result: A51R homologs from different poxviruses (with 30-90% amino acid identity to VACV-WR A51R) all enhanced VSV gene expression to similar levels, indicating that the ability to overcome LD652 restriction to VSV infection is a conserved function of distantly-related A51R homologs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this conservation analysis. The manuscript is noted to 'identify multiple targets for A51R, which will be useful for future detailed characterizations of its mechanisms of action,' implicitly accepting the data showing functional conservation across A51R homologs from different poxvirus genera.

results.result: A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in multiple Lepidopteran cell lines (LdEP, Sf9, GV-1) but not in Drosophila melanogaster-derived DL1 cells, suggesting A51R targets restrictions specific to Lepidoptera.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings about cell-type specificity without challenge. The observation that A51R works in Lepidopteran but not Dipteran cells is consistent with reviewers' statement that 'A51R overcomes immunity mechanisms that are shared between Lepidopterans and mammals but absent or easily antagonized in Dipteran insects,' indicating acceptance of the differential activity across insect orders.
